Title: Meningitis in the Neonate.

Journal/Date: Current treatment options in neurology (2002)

MeSH Keywords: None listed


--- ABSTRACT ---
Group B beta-hemolytic streptococci and Escherichia coli strains account for approximately two thirds of all cases of neonatal meningitis, while bacteria that typically account for meningitis in older age groups (Haemophilus influenzae type B, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae) are infrequent causes of meningitis in the neonatal population. As with other medical problems in neonates, signs and symptoms of bacterial infection of the central nervous system are generally few in number and nonspecific in nature. Manifestations that can suggest meningitis, as well as other serious illnesses, include temperature instability, lethargy, respiratory distress, poor feeding, vomiting, and diarrhea. Signs suggestive of meningeal irritation, including stiff neck, bulging fontanelle, convulsions, and opisthotonus, occur only in a minority of neonates with bacterial meningitis and cannot be relied on solely to identify such patients. Ampicillin and either gentamicin or cefotaxime are recommended for initial empiric therapy of neonatal meningitis. When the results of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture and susceptibilities are known, therapy can be narrowed to cover the specific pathogen identified. In general, penicillin G or ampicillin is preferred for group B streptococcal meningitis, ampicillin for Listeria monocytogenes meningitis, and ampicillin plus either an aminoglycoside or cefotaxime for gram-negative meningitis. For the very low birth weight neonate who has been in the nursery for a prolonged period of time, organisms such as enterococci and gentamicin-resistant gram-negative enteric bacilli must also be considered. In patients with long-term vascular catheters, Staphylococcus aureus or coagulase-negative staphylococci must also be considered. Empiric combinations of antibiotics for such patients would include ampicillin or vancomycin, plus amikacin or cefotaxime. All neonates should undergo repeat CSF examination and culture at 48 to 72 hours after initiation of therapy. If organisms are observed on gram stain, modification of the therapeutic regimen should be considered, and neuroimaging should be performed. In general, therapy should be continued for 14 to 21 days for neonatal meningitis caused by group B streptococci or L. monocytogenes, and for at least 21 days for disease caused by gram-negative enteric bacilli. All patients with neonatal meningitis should have hearing and development monitored serially. The first audiologic evaluation should occur 4 to 6 weeks after resolution of the meningitis.

This covers Group B Streptococcus and Listeria (ampicillin) and E. coli/other enteric gram-negative bacilli (cefotaxime); cefotaxime is preferred over gentamicin when meningitis is present because of better CNS penetration. Ampicillin plus gentamicin is an accepted neonatal empiric alternative in some references, but cefotaxime is the closer match for confirmed/suspected meningitis.

source_tools.relevance: Neonatal meningitis review explicitly recommends ampicillin plus either gentamicin or cefotaxime empirically and specifies pathogen-directed coverage; cefotaxime is included for gram-negative meningitis.
Recent review states that when meningitis is suspected, cefotaxime should substitute for the aminoglycoside; another neonatal meningitis report notes gentamicin has limited CNS penetration.
Search results identify GBS, E. coli, and Listeria as key neonatal pathogens and support ampicillin/cefotaxime-based empiric therapy.

key_findings.finding: Coverage comparison: ampicillin is necessary for GBS and Listeria monocytogenes; cefotaxime supplies strong coverage for E. coli and other susceptible gram-negative bacilli and has activity against S. pneumoniae. key_findings.finding: Acyclovir is not routinely required when the presentation is strongly bacterial by CSF and there are no vesicular lesions, seizures, disseminated disease, or other compelling HSV features. However, HSV risk is age-sensitive: a study of infants under 90 days recommends considering empiric acyclovir for suspected CNS infection in the first 21 days even without CSF pleocytosis, but explicitly makes an exception when CSF parameters are suggestive of bacterial meningitis. Thus, in this case it would generally be withheld initially while obtaining HSV PCR/testing, with a low threshold to add it if the clinical picture evolves or HSV risk factors emerge.

source_tools.relevance: PICNIC study conclusion recommends empiric HSV therapy in suspected CNS infection during the first 21 days, but expressly excludes cases whose CSF parameters suggest bacterial meningitis; seizures and extra-CNS disease were more associated with HSV.
HSV-focused search found that empiric acyclovir is used in high-risk congenital HSV contexts, supporting risk-based rather than universal addition.

key_findings.finding: Therefore, among typical answer choices, select “ampicillin plus cefotaxime” (often dosed using neonatal meningitis dosing and adjusted for gestational/postnatal age and renal function). Do not select a regimen based only on ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, which is aimed at older infants/children and does not reliably provide the neonatal Listeria coverage supplied by ampicillin.
